title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services

reading.body:
Scammers created deepfake videos and fake social media profiles using AI to impersonate a Miami immigration attorney, falsely advertising services like US residency assistance for specific fees. The fake profiles directed vulnerable immigrants to WhatsApp and fake contracts designed to extract payment. This is a failure of social media platforms to prevent impersonation at scale, where thousands of fraudulent accounts remained visible before removal by a hired anti-piracy company.

The deployment failure occurred in the absence of human verification of identity and credentials on platforms where the deepfakes circulated. The scam targeted people seeking legal services and unable to easily verify legitimacy through standard channels. What would have caught this earlier: platforms requiring identity verification before allowing profiles to offer legal services, automated detection of deepfake video content, and real-time flagging of accounts impersonating real individuals.

It is not established who created the deepfakes, whether the scammers used publicly available AI tools or developed their own systems, or what specific AI techniques generated the fake videos.

reports.title: Scammers steal identity of renowned Miami attorney to target immigrants on social media
South Florida immigration attorney says AI scammers are using his identity to target immigrants
Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
Legal resident loses thousands seeking citizenship to AI immigration attorney

summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the target of artificial intelligence scammers who are using deepfake videos and fake social media profiles to defraud vulnerable immigrants. The criminals create AI-generated images and videos showing Leal offering immigration services he never provides, including US residency assistance for $2,200. Leal first discovered the scheme when potential clients began calling his office about services advertised on social media. The fraud has escalated dramatically over the past three months, with scammers directing victims through WhatsApp and fake contracts.

Leal's office hired an anti-piracy company that has successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake profiles across social media platforms, including 3,500 on TikTok, 2,400 on Facebook, and 544 on Instagram. The scams often include testimonials from fake former clients claiming to have received legal status through his help. Leal warns immigrants to be cautious of requests for payment through apps like Venmo, Zelle, or Cash App, and to verify anyone offering legal services online. He plans to contact local and federal authorities to investigate the origin of the fraud.
